Casement
KAYSS-ment
noun
Probably from encasement, a hollow moulding or frame, related to case, from Latin capsa, a chest — a hinged window-frame or latticed opening. It renders Hebrew eshnab (H822), the pierced window-screen; a hapax legomenon in the KJV at Proverbs 7:6.

Biblical Definition

Casement appears but once in the KJV, in the seventh chapter of Proverbs, where the wise man sets himself as a watcher: “For at the window of my house I looked through my casement” (Pro 7:6). From that lattice he beholds among the simple ones a young man void of understanding, passing through the street near the corner of the strange woman’s house in the twilight, and going after her “as an ox goeth to the slaughter” until a dart strike through his liver. The casement is the vantage of watchful wisdom, the framed opening through which the discerning eye observes the folly and ruin of the careless. Scripture often sets a watcher at such a window: Abimelech “looked out at a window, and saw… Isaac was sporting with Rebekah” (Gen 26:8); Michal “looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD… and she despised him in her heart” (2Sa 6:16); and the Beloved “looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice” (Son 2:9). The window is a place of seeing, and what a heart sees there reveals the heart itself — the wise man reads a warning, Michal reads only contempt, the Beloved offers a gracious sight. Through his casement the sage teaches by observation: he takes the ruin of a fool for a lesson, that we might learn wisdom at another’s cost and not our own. Blessed is the man who watches at wisdom’s casement, keeping his feet from the strange woman’s door because he has seen, through the lattice, where that road ends.

Webster 1828 Definition

A window-frame or latticed opening that swings on hinges; the casement through which the wise man watched.

CASEMENT, noun. A window, or part of a window, opening upon hinges; a hollow frame or moulding for a window.

A latticed or framed opening in a wall through which one may look out or in.

In Scripture, the casement of the wise man’s house, through which he beheld the simple young man going to ruin (Pro 7:6).

A hapax legomenon in the KJV, occurring only at Proverbs 7:6, rendering the Hebrew for a latticed window.

By extension, any frame that encloses or a hollow moulding, as in architecture.

Key Scripture

Pro 7:6 — "For at the window of my house I looked through my casement,"

Gen 26:8 — "And it came to pass, when he had been there a long time, that Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and, behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife."

2Sa 6:16 — "And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart."

Son 2:9 — "My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice."

Modern Corruption

A latticed window of the eastern house, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the watchful wisdom that learns from another’s ruin.

expand to see more

The temptation the casement rebukes is heedlessness — the refusal to watch, to observe, to learn wisdom at another’s cost. The young man of Proverbs 7 was void of understanding because he did not see where his path led; the wise man at his casement did see, and set it down for our warning. An age that scorns instruction and must touch every fire for itself has forgotten the grace of learning through a watchful window rather than through one’s own destruction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is watchful wisdom — the discipline of observing the ways of folly and the ends of sin, and taking warning before the dart strikes through the liver. Scripture sets a watcher at the window that we might learn to keep our own feet from the strange woman’s door, saved from ruin by a lesson seen and heeded rather than suffered.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew eshnab (H822), a latticed window; a KJV hapax at Proverbs 7:6, rendered elsewhere “lattice.”

Hebrew eshnab (H822) — a latticed window or casement; only twice in Scripture (Jdg 5:28; Pro 7:6)

Rendered “casement” only at Proverbs 7:6, a hapax legomenon in the KJV

Likely from encasement, a hollow frame or moulding, related to Latin capsa, a chest

The vantage of the wise man watching the ruin of the simple young man

One of Scripture’s several windows of watching (Gen 26:8; 2Sa 6:16; Son 2:9)

Usage

"Through his casement the wise man watched the young fool go as an ox to the slaughter."

"The window reveals the heart: Michal saw David and despised, the sage saw folly and warned."

"Blessed is he who learns wisdom at the casement rather than at the cost of his own ruin."
